pairs.source_text: decessitque Pyrgis morbo aquae intercutis, sublato filio Nerone ex Agrippina Germanico genita.
pairs.question: Quae fuit mater Neronis imperatoris?
pairs.question_en: Who was the mother of the emperor Nero?
pairs.derivation: Names Nero's mother and her father: 'ex Agrippina Germanico genita' (Agrippina the Younger, daughter of Germanicus). Entity-anchored to Nero; single-name answer with the Germanicus lineage supported verbatim. Closed-book: among the best-known Julio-Claudian relationships.

pairs.source_text: Nero natus est Anti post VIIII. mensem quam Tiberius excessit, XVIII. Kal. Ian.
pairs.question: Quo in oppido natum esse Neronem Suetonius tradit?
pairs.question_en: In what town does Suetonius say Nero was born?
pairs.derivation: Birthplace fact, supported by 'Nero natus est Anti' (locative of Antium, spelled 'Anti' in this Latin Library file). Indirect statement (natum esse) under tradit; place answer, entity-anchored to Nero. Closed-book: Antium is the famous birthplace of Nero.

pairs.source_text: Undecimo aetatis anno a Claudio adoptatus est Annaeoque Senecae iam tunc senatori in disciplinam traditus.
pairs.question: A quo principe Nero adoptatus est?
pairs.question_en: By which emperor was Nero adopted?
pairs.derivation: Supported by 'a Claudio adoptatus est'; Nero, adopted by the emperor Claudius (AD 50, in his eleventh year), later succeeded him. Entity-anchored, single-name answer, closed-book famous.

pairs.source_text: Nec multo post duxit uxorem Octaviam ediditque pro Claudi salute circenses et venationem.
pairs.question: Quam primam uxorem Nero duxit?
pairs.question_en: Whom did Nero take as his first wife?
pairs.derivation: Supported by 'duxit uxorem Octaviam' (Octavia, daughter of Claudius). That she was his first wife is confirmed at ch. 35 ('Uxores praeter Octaviam duas postea duxit'). Entity-anchored, single-name answer.

pairs.source_text: afflicti suppliciis Christiani, genus hominum superstitionis novae ac maleficae;
pairs.question: Quod genus hominum Nerone principe suppliciis affectum esse Suetonius refert?
pairs.question_en: What kind of people does Suetonius report were punished under Nero?
pairs.derivation: Supported verbatim by 'afflicti suppliciis Christiani'. Indirect statement (affectum esse genus) under refert. The Neronian persecution of Christians is a famous, closed-book fact; entity-anchored to Nero and the Christiani.

pairs.source_text: Non in alia re tamen damnosior quam in aedificando domum a Palatio Esquilias usque fecit, quam primo transitoriam, mox incendio absumptam restitutamque auream nominavit.
pairs.question: Quo nomine Nero domum suam ingentem a Palatio ad Esquilias porrectam appellavit?
pairs.question_en: By what name did Nero call his huge house stretching from the Palatine to the Esquiline?
pairs.derivation: Supported by 'auream nominavit'. The Domus Aurea, his palace from the Palatine to the Esquiline. Entity-anchored to Nero, short name answer, closed-book famous.

pairs.source_text: Britannicum non minus aemulatione vocis, quae illi iucundior suppetebat, quam metu ne quandoque apud hominum gratiam paterna memoria praevaleret, veneno adgressus est.
pairs.question: Quo modo Nero Britannicum, Claudii filium, e medio sustulit?
pairs.question_en: By what means did Nero do away with Britannicus, the son of Claudius?
pairs.derivation: Supported by 'veneno adgressus est'. Britannicus (Claudius's son and Nero's adoptive brother) was poisoned; the means is the verifiable fact. Entity-anchored, short answer, closed-book famous. (The poison was supplied by Lucusta, named in the same chapter.)

pairs.question: Quam propinquam suam Nero parricidio sustulit, ut Suetonius narrat?
pairs.question_en: Which of his relatives did Nero kill by parricide, according to Suetonius?
pairs.derivation: Supported by 'parricido matris' (parricide of his mother), with the whole chapter narrating the murder of Agrippina. Entity-anchored to Nero and his mother; the matricide is among the most famous facts about Nero. (source_text retains the OCR slip 'parricido'/'amitaee' from the Latin Library file.)

pairs.source_text: Senecam praeceptorem ad necem compulit, quamvis saepe commeatum petenti bonisque cedenti persancte iurasset suspectum se frustra periturumque potius quam nociturum ei.
pairs.question: Quem praeceptorem suum Nero ad necem compulit?
pairs.question_en: Which of his teachers did Nero force to his death?
pairs.derivation: Supported by 'Senecam praeceptorem ad necem compulit', which names Seneca both as Nero's teacher (praeceptor) and as forced to suicide. Entity-anchored, single-name answer, closed-book famous.

pairs.source_text: Uxores praeter Octaviam duas postea duxit, Poppaeam Sabinam quaestorio patre natam et equiti Romano antea nuptam, deinde Statiliam Messalinam Tauri bis consulis ac triumphalis abneptem.
pairs.question: Quas duas uxores Nero praeter Octaviam postea duxit?
pairs.question_en: Which two wives besides Octavia did Nero later marry?
pairs.derivation: Supported verbatim: 'praeter Octaviam duas postea duxit, Poppaeam Sabinam ... deinde Statiliam Messalinam'. Entity-anchored to Nero, two named answers fully supported. Closed-book naming fact.

pairs.source_text: Poppaeam duodecimo die post divortium Octaviae in matrimonium acceptam dilexit unice; et tamen ipsam quoque ictu calcis occidit, quod se ex aurigatione sero reversum gravida et aegra conviciis incesserat.
pairs.question: Quo modo Nero Poppaeam uxorem interfecit?
pairs.question_en: How did Nero kill his wife Poppaea?
pairs.derivation: Supported by 'ipsam quoque ictu calcis occidit'. Concrete, verifiable manner of death of the pregnant Poppaea; entity-anchored to Nero and Poppaea, short answer. Closed-book, widely reported.

pairs.source_text: Per sex dies septemque noctes ea clade saevitum est ad monumentorum bustorumque deversoria plebe compulsa.
pairs.question: Per quot dies noctesque incendium illud Romae, Nerone principe, saevit?
pairs.question_en: For how many days and nights did that fire of Rome rage in Nero's principate?
pairs.answer_en: For six days and seven nights.
pairs.derivation: Duration of the Great Fire of Rome (AD 64), supported by 'Per sex dies septemque noctes ea clade saevitum est'. Number fact, entity-anchored to Nero's reign, closed-book famous.

pairs.source_text: Hoc incendium e turre Maecenantina prospectans laetusque 'flammae', ut aiebat, 'pulchritudine' Halosin Ilii in illo suo scaenico habitu decantavit.
pairs.question: Quod carmen Nero, incendium urbis e turre Maecenatiana prospectans, decantavit?
pairs.question_en: What song did Nero sing while watching the fire of the city from the tower of Maecenas?
pairs.derivation: Supported by 'Halosin Ilii ... decantavit'. The famous image of Nero singing 'The Capture of Troy' while watching Rome burn. Entity-anchored, single titled answer, closed-book. (source_text keeps the file's spelling 'Maecenantina'; inner quotes normalized to single quotes.)

pairs.source_text: Talem principem paulo minus quattuordecim annos perpessus terrarum orbis tandem destituit, initium facientibus Gallis duce Iulio Vindice, Qui tum eam provinciam pro praetore optinebat.
pairs.question: Per quot fere annos Nero principatum tenuit, ut Suetonius tradit?
pairs.question_en: For about how many years did Nero hold the principate, according to Suetonius?
pairs.answer_en: A little less than fourteen years.
pairs.derivation: Length of reign, supported by 'paulo minus quattuordecim annos'; corroborated at ch. 51 ('per quattuordecim annos'). Number fact, entity-anchored to Nero, closed-book.

pairs.source_text: Talem principem paulo minus quattuordecim annos perpessus terrarum orbis tandem destituit, initium facientibus Gallis duce Iulio Vindice, Qui tum eam provinciam pro praetore optinebat.
pairs.question: Quo duce Galli adversus Neronem defecerunt?
pairs.question_en: Under which leader did the Gauls revolt against Nero?
pairs.derivation: Supported by 'initium facientibus Gallis duce Iulio Vindice'. The Gallic revolt that began Nero's downfall was led by Julius Vindex. Entity-anchored, single-name answer, closed-book.

pairs.source_text: flens ad singula atque identidem dictitans: 'Qualis artifex pereo!'
pairs.question: Quae verba Nero moriturus identidem dictitavit?
pairs.question_en: What words did Nero repeatedly utter as he was about to die?
pairs.answer_en: What an artist perishes in me!
pairs.derivation: Nero's most famous saying, reported verbatim by Suetonius: 'Qualis artifex pereo!'. Fact-seeking (which words), entity-anchored to the dying Nero, closed-book famous.

pairs.source_text: ferrum iugulo adegit iuvante Epaphrodito a libellis.
pairs.question: Quo modo Nero sibi mortem conscivit?
pairs.question_en: How did Nero bring about his own death?
pairs.answer_en: By driving a sword into his throat.
pairs.derivation: Supported by 'ferrum iugulo adegit', with the aid of his secretary Epaphroditus ('iuvante Epaphrodito a libellis'). Manner of death is the verifiable fact; entity-anchored to Nero, closed-book famous.

pairs.source_text: Obiit tricensimo et secundo aetatis anno, die quo quondam Octaviam interemerat, tantumque gaudium publice praebuit, ut plebs pilleata tota urbe discurreret.
pairs.question: Quoto aetatis anno Nero obiit, ut Suetonius tradit?
pairs.question_en: In which year of his age did Nero die, according to Suetonius?
pairs.derivation: Age-at-death fact, supported by 'Obiit tricensimo et secundo aetatis anno'. Number/ordinal answer, entity-anchored to Nero, closed-book.
